title: Donnie Iris, Pittsburgh Music Icon, Passes Away at 71 – CBS News Reports】
body:
The world of rock‑and‑roll lost one of its most enduring regional icons on Monday when Don Iris, the Pittsburgh‑born singer‑songwriter best known for the 1980 hit “Ah! Leah!,” died at the age of 83. The news was confirmed by former bandmate Mark Avsec, who said Iris had been battling a serious bladder condition for several years. The musician’s passing marks the end of a career that spanned more than five decades and helped shape the sound of the Steel City’s vibrant music scene.

Born John Donovan Iris in the small town of Ellwood City, Pennsylvania, the artist grew up immersed in the working‑class culture that would later color his lyrics and stage persona. After early stints with local groups such as The Jaggerz—who scored a national hit with “The Rapper” in 1970—he formed the band The Innocent and later the power‑pop outfit Wild Cherry. It was with Wild Cherry that Iris first tasted broader success, delivering the 1979 single “Play the Game” and laying the groundwork for his signature blend of melodic rock, new‑wave synths, and heartfelt vocal delivery.

The turning point came in 1980 when Iris, now fronting his own band Don Iris and the Cruisers, released “Ah! Leah!” on the MCA label. The song’s soaring chorus and instantly recognizable guitar riff propelled it to No. 29 on the Billboard Hot 100 and cemented Iris as a household name across the Midwest and Northeast. The track’s enduring popularity has kept it in rotation on classic‑rock radio stations for more than four decades, and it remains a staple at sporting events, local festivals, and karaoke nights in the region.

Beyond the chart‑topping single, Iris built a prolific catalog that blended rock anthems with tender ballads, earning a devoted fan base that extended well beyond his native Pennsylvania. Albums such as *Back on the Streets* (1980), *The High and the Mighty* (1982), and *Out of the Blue* (1992) showcased his knack for crafting catchy hooks while exploring themes of love, perseverance, and small‑town pride. His live performances—often featuring a full band, energetic lighting, and his unmistakable raspy voice—became legendary in the area’s club circuit, drawing crowds that spanned generations.

Industry peers and local musicians have lauded Iris not only for his artistic contributions but also for his mentorship of younger talent. He frequently opened his home studio to up‑and‑coming acts, offering guidance on songwriting, production, and navigating the business side of music. In interviews, he emphasized the importance of staying true to one’s roots, a philosophy that resonated with artists who later cited him as an influence on their own work. His commitment to community was evident in numerous charitable performances, including benefit concerts for local hospitals and youth music programs.

Iris’s death arrives at a moment when the music industry is reflecting on the legacy of artists who helped define regional sounds in an era before streaming homogenized global playlists. While his name may not be as instantly recognizable as some national superstars, his impact on the cultural fabric of western Pennsylvania is undeniable. Fans have already begun gathering at his former haunts—such as the historic Carnegie Music Hall in downtown Pittsburgh—to share memories, play his recordings, and celebrate a life that brought a distinct voice to the American rock narrative.

As tributes pour in and radio stations prepare special programming in his honor, the broader music community is poised to revisit Iris’s extensive body of work, ensuring that “Ah! Leah!” and the rest of his catalog continue to inspire future generations. The enduring appeal of his songs suggests that, even as the industry evolves, the authentic storytelling and melodic craftsmanship that defined Don Iris’s career will remain a touchstone for artists seeking to capture the spirit of their own hometowns.
